objective: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
question: A senior engineer at a fintech company has Claude Code reliably following the team's error-handling and logging conventions. A new hire clones the same repository, but Claude Code ignores those conventions entirely in her sessions. The senior engineer runs /memory and sees the conventions load from ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on his machine. What is the root cause and the right fix?
options: The conventions live in the senior engineer's user-level CLAUDE.md, which is not shared via version control; move them into the project-level CLAUDE.md in the repository
The new hire's Claude Code installation is outdated and cannot read memory files; have her reinstall the CLI and re-clone the repository to refresh configuration
User-level CLAUDE.md files require explicit activation per project; have the new hire run /memory in the repository once to register the senior engineer's file
The conventions should be copied into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on each teammate's machine so every developer carries an identical personal configuration
optionExplanations: Correct. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is user-level configuration: it applies only to that user and is never shared with teammates through version control. Team-wide conventions belong in the project-level CLAUDE.md checked into the repository, where every clone receives them automatically.

Tempting because a fresh environment often explains odd behavior, but nothing here indicates a broken installation. The reasoning error is blaming the tool when the configuration hierarchy explains the symptom exactly: user-level files simply never travel with the repository.

Tempting because /memory is genuinely the diagnostic command for loaded memory files, but it only shows what is loaded — it cannot register another user's home-directory file. This misreads a read-only diagnostic as an activation mechanism that does not exist.

Tempting because it would technically work at first, but manually copying files to every home directory recreates the exact drift problem: copies fall out of sync, new hires are missed, and nothing is reviewed or versioned. Shared knowledge belongs in project scope, not duplicated per user.
principle: user-level configuration is never shared via version control
relatedConcept: The CLAUDE.md hierarchy (user, project, directory) determines who receives which instructions and how they propagate.
overallExplanation: User-level configuration is never shared via version control. The CLAUDE.md hierarchy (user, project, directory) determines who receives which instructions — team conventions belong at project level.

objective: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
question: A healthcare SaaS company maintains a monorepo with six packages. The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 2,400 lines covering API standards, frontend conventions, database migration rules, and deployment procedures for every package. Developers report Claude Code behaving inconsistently, and every session burns tokens on standards irrelevant to the package being edited. Package maintainers know best which standards apply to their code. What is the most maintainable restructuring?
options: Ask each developer to maintain a personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md containing only the standards for the packages they usually work on
Split the standards into focused files and have each package's CLAUDE.md use @import to include only the standards files relevant to that package
Keep the monolithic root CLAUDE.md but add a table of contents and instruct Claude to read only the sections that apply to the current task
Convert the entire standards document into a skill so that developers can invoke it on demand whenever they need the team's conventions
optionExplanations: Tempting because it reduces each session's context, but it moves shared standards into unshared user-level files, guaranteeing drift between developers and leaving new hires with nothing. It solves token waste by abandoning consistency, which is the wrong trade-off.

Correct. The @import syntax keeps CLAUDE.md modular: standards live in focused external files, and each package's CLAUDE.md imports only what applies, curated by the maintainers who hold the domain knowledge. Sessions load relevant context without the monolith's noise.

Tempting because it requires no restructuring, but a table of contents relies on the model choosing to skip sections — the full file still loads and consumes tokens, and inference-based section selection is exactly the inconsistency being reported. It treats the symptom, not the structure.

Tempting because skills reduce always-loaded context, but universal coding standards must apply to every session automatically, not only when a developer remembers to invoke a skill. On-demand invocation is the wrong loading model for always-applicable conventions.
principle: modularize CLAUDE.md with @import instead of growing a monolith
relatedConcept: @import and .claude/rules/ let large teams keep instructions scoped, curated, and token-efficient.
overallExplanation: Modularize CLAUDE.md with @import instead of growing a monolith. Scoped imports curated by package maintainers keep every session's context relevant and token-efficient.

objective: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
question: A retail platform team uses Claude Code daily. They have two assets to encode: naming and error-handling conventions that must shape every piece of generated code, and a multi-step release-notes workflow that a developer runs roughly once per sprint. The architect must decide where each belongs so both work reliably for the whole team. What is the correct placement?
options: Put both in the project CLAUDE.md so nothing depends on developers remembering to invoke anything during a session
Put both in .claude/skills/ so each is versioned, documented, and loaded only when a developer explicitly needs it
Put the conventions in the project CLAUDE.md and package the release-notes workflow as a project-scoped skill invoked on demand
Put the conventions in each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and the release-notes workflow in ~/.claude/commands/ for fast personal access
optionExplanations: Tempting because CLAUDE.md guarantees the content is always present, but stuffing an occasional multi-step workflow into always-loaded memory wastes tokens in every session for something used once a sprint. Always-loaded scope should be reserved for universal standards.

Tempting because skills are versioned and shareable, but conventions placed in a skill only apply when someone invokes it — generated code in ordinary sessions would ignore the team's standards. Universal rules need the always-loaded mechanism, not on-demand invocation.

Correct. The dividing line is loading model: CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded universal standards that must shape every session, while skills are for on-demand, task-specific workflows. Project scope keeps both shared through version control.

Tempting because personal configuration feels convenient, but user-level files and ~/.claude/commands/ are not shared via version control, so teammates and new hires get neither the conventions nor the workflow. Team assets belong in project scope.
principle: always-loaded standards go in CLAUDE.md; on-demand workflows become skills
relatedConcept: Choosing between skills and CLAUDE.md is a decision about loading model: universal context versus task-specific invocation.
overallExplanation: Always-loaded standards go in CLAUDE.md; on-demand workflows become skills. The choice is about loading model — universal context versus task-specific invocation — with project scope for anything the team shares.

objective: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
question: A platform team is building a codebase-analysis skill in .claude/skills/. Two problems surfaced in testing: the skill's exploration dumps thousands of lines of discovery output into the main conversation, drowning the session's context, and during one run the skill modified source files when it should only ever write its report into docs/. Which two SKILL.md frontmatter configurations address these problems? (Choose two.)
options: Set context: fork so the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context and its verbose output does not pollute the main conversation
Configure allowed-tools to restrict the skill to the file-write operations it legitimately needs, preventing destructive modifications
Add argument-hint so developers are prompted for the required parameters whenever they invoke the skill without arguments
Move the skill to ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name so each developer runs a personal variant that cannot affect teammates
optionExplanations: Correct. context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, so verbose exploratory output stays out of the main session — exactly the mechanism for skills that produce heavy discovery output like codebase analysis.

Correct. allowed-tools in skill frontmatter restricts which tools the skill may use during execution; limiting it to the write operations it needs is the deterministic way to prevent the destructive source-file edits observed in testing.

Tempting because argument-hint is a real frontmatter option and improves usability, but it only prompts for missing parameters at invocation time. It does nothing about context pollution or unrestricted tool access, which are the two failures described.

Tempting because personal variants in ~/.claude/skills/ are a legitimate customization pattern, but it addresses neither problem: the verbose output and the destructive writes would follow the skill wherever it lives, and the team loses the shared, versioned skill.
principle: frontmatter is the control surface: fork for isolation, allowed-tools for safety
relatedConcept: SKILL.md frontmatter (context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint) configures how a skill executes, not just what it does.
overallExplanation: Frontmatter is the control surface: context: fork isolates verbose output in a sub-agent, and allowed-tools deterministically restricts what the skill can touch during execution.

objective: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
question: An infrastructure team at an insurance company keeps Terraform code under terraform/ with detailed conventions: module structure, state-management rules, and tagging standards. Today those conventions sit in the root CLAUDE.md, so they load into every session — including frontend work where they are irrelevant — inflating token usage and occasionally bleeding Terraform advice into unrelated tasks. How should the team scope these conventions?
options: Create a .claude/rules/ file containing the Terraform conventions with YAML frontmatter declaring paths: ["terraform/**/*"] so it loads only when editing matching files
Move the Terraform conventions into a skill that infrastructure engineers invoke at the start of any session where they expect to touch Terraform code
Keep the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md but preface the section with a note telling Claude to apply it only when the current task involves Terraform
Ask infrastructure engineers to add the conventions to their personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files since they are the only developers who need them
optionExplanations: Correct. Rule files in .claude/rules/ with a YAML frontmatter paths field activate conditionally: the conventions load only when Claude edits files matching the glob, which cuts irrelevant context and token usage in every non-Terraform session while keeping the rules versioned and shared.

Tempting because a skill would keep the content out of unrelated sessions, but it depends on an engineer remembering to invoke it — forget once and Terraform work proceeds without the conventions. Conditional loading should be automatic and path-driven, not memory-driven.

Tempting because it needs no restructuring, but the full section still loads and consumes tokens in every session, and applying it 'only when relevant' relies on model inference — precisely the bleed-through behavior the team is already seeing.

Tempting because it targets the right audience, but user-level files are not shared via version control, so the conventions drift per engineer and vanish for new hires. It also still loads the content into all of those engineers' sessions, Terraform or not.
principle: path-scoped rules load conventions only when matching files are edited
relatedConcept: .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter paths globs gives deterministic, token-efficient conditional loading.
overallExplanation: Path-scoped rules load conventions only when matching files are edited. YAML frontmatter globs in .claude/rules/ make convention loading deterministic and token-efficient instead of inference-based.

objective: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
question: A media company's codebase co-locates tests with source files: Player.test.tsx sits beside Player.tsx across dozens of directories. The team created .claude/rules/testing.md with frontmatter paths: ["src/tests/**"], but the testing conventions almost never load because very few tests live under src/tests/. Claude keeps generating tests that ignore the team's mocking and naming standards. What change fixes the conditional loading?
options: Change the frontmatter glob to match test files by type wherever they live, for example paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"], so the rule activates for co-located tests
Place a CLAUDE.md file containing the testing conventions in every directory that currently contains at least one co-located test file
Remove the paths frontmatter entirely so testing.md loads unconditionally into every session regardless of which files are being edited
Relocate all test files into src/tests/ so the existing glob matches them and the directory structure mirrors the rule configuration
optionExplanations: Correct. Glob-pattern rules can target files by type regardless of directory location — exactly the advantage of path-specific rules over directory-bound configuration when conventions apply to files spread throughout a codebase. A **/*.test.tsx pattern matches every co-located test.

Tempting because directory-level CLAUDE.md files do scope instructions, but tests are spread across dozens of directories: you would duplicate the conventions everywhere, keep every copy in sync, and update the set each time tests appear in a new directory. Glob rules exist to avoid this.

Tempting because it guarantees the conventions are present, but unconditional loading throws away the entire benefit of path scoping — every non-testing session pays the token cost and carries irrelevant context. The glob was wrong; the mechanism was not.

Tempting because it makes the existing rule work, but restructuring the whole codebase to satisfy a one-line configuration inverts the relationship between code and tooling. Co-located tests are a deliberate, common convention; the rule should adapt to the code.
principle: glob rules follow file type; directory files follow location
relatedConcept: Path-specific rules beat directory-level CLAUDE.md when conventions span files scattered across the codebase.
overallExplanation: Glob rules follow file type; directory files follow location. When conventions apply to files scattered across the codebase, a frontmatter glob like **/*.test.tsx is the maintainable scoping mechanism.

objective: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
question: A logistics company must migrate its Node.js services from a deprecated HTTP client library to a supported one. The migration touches 45+ files, and there are two viable integration approaches with different retry and connection-pooling implications for production infrastructure. An engineer asks whether to just start editing files with Claude Code. What should you advise?
options: Use plan mode to explore the codebase and compare the two integration approaches, then execute the chosen plan with direct implementation
Use direct execution file by file, since migrations are mechanical and each file's changes will reveal which integration approach fits best
Use direct execution with a comprehensive upfront prompt specifying exactly how every one of the 45+ files should be modified in a single pass
Split the work across parallel Claude Code sessions, one per service, so each session's context stays small enough to finish without planning
optionExplanations: Correct. This task has plan mode's signature traits: large-scale multi-file changes, multiple valid approaches, and architectural implications for infrastructure. Planning first enables safe exploration and a deliberate approach choice, then direct execution implements the committed plan.

Tempting because migrations feel mechanical, but the approach decision has infrastructure-wide retry and pooling consequences — discovering it mid-migration means rework across every file already edited. Incremental execution defers exactly the decision that must come first.

Tempting because thorough instructions feel like planning, but it assumes you already know the right approach without exploring the code, and a 45-file single pass leaves no room to validate the architectural choice. It is planning's paperwork without its investigation.

Tempting because parallel sessions do manage context size, but the core risk is an unmade architectural decision, not context exhaustion. Parallelizing before choosing an approach multiplies the rework if the wrong integration pattern is picked.
principle: plan mode for architectural, multi-file, multiple-valid-approach work
relatedConcept: Plan mode enables safe exploration and design before committing to changes, preventing costly rework on large migrations.
overallExplanation: Plan mode fits architectural, multi-file work with multiple valid approaches. Explore and decide first, then execute — the pattern that prevents costly rework on large migrations.

objective: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
question: During a multi-phase modernization task, an engineer uses Claude Code to survey a sprawling legacy codebase before implementation. The discovery phase floods the session with file listings, grep output, and long file reads; by the time implementation starts, the context window is nearly exhausted and the model has begun losing earlier findings. Which technique best preserves the main conversation for the phases that follow?
options: Delegate the verbose discovery work to the Explore subagent so only summarized findings return to the main conversation
Skip the discovery phase and move straight to direct execution, reading individual files only at the moment each change requires them
Restart the session at the end of discovery and rely on the model to re-derive the important findings during implementation
Ask Claude to keep its discovery output brief so that file listings and search results consume fewer tokens in the main session
optionExplanations: Correct. The Explore subagent exists precisely to isolate verbose discovery output: exploration happens in a separate context and only summaries return, preserving the main conversation's window for planning and implementation across a multi-phase task.

Tempting because just-in-time reading limits context growth, but abandoning discovery on a sprawling legacy codebase forfeits the system-level understanding the modernization needs — changes get made without knowing what they affect. It trades context safety for rework risk.

Tempting because a fresh session does reset the window, but the findings were the valuable product of discovery; discarding them and hoping the model re-derives everything repeats the expensive exploration and reintroduces the same flooding problem.

Tempting because brevity instructions reduce some verbosity, but tool results like file reads and grep matches enter context at their actual size regardless of how tersely the model narrates them. Prompted brevity cannot isolate discovery output the way a subagent can.
principle: isolate verbose discovery in the Explore subagent, keep summaries in main context
relatedConcept: Plan mode pairs with the Explore subagent so investigation can be thorough without exhausting the main conversation's window.
overallExplanation: Isolate verbose discovery in the Explore subagent and keep only summaries in the main context. Thorough investigation and a healthy context window stop being a trade-off when exploration runs in its own context.

objective: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
question: A data engineer asks Claude Code to write a script converting legacy customer records to a new schema. She describes the transformation in careful prose — three paragraphs covering field renames, date reformatting, and address splitting — but each attempt interprets the rules differently: one run splits addresses on commas, the next on line breaks. What is the most effective way to communicate the expected transformation?
options: Provide 2-3 concrete input/output example pairs showing exactly how representative legacy records should look after conversion
Rewrite the prose specification with stricter language, numbering every rule and warning Claude not to deviate from the stated steps
Start a fresh session for each attempt so earlier misinterpretations cannot contaminate the next generation of the script
Ask Claude to restate the specification in its own words before coding, and correct any misreadings before implementation begins
optionExplanations: Correct. When prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently, concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate the expected transformation — a real record and its converted form pin down ambiguities (like the address delimiter) that no prose phrasing settles.

Tempting because stricter wording feels more precise, but the failures show the prose itself is ambiguous — 'split the address' still does not say on what. More emphatic prose multiplies words without adding the disambiguating information an example carries.

Tempting because contamination across turns is a real phenomenon, but the runs already varied independently — the inconsistency comes from an ambiguous specification, not polluted context. Fresh sessions would reroll the dice on the same vague prose.

Tempting because a restating step can catch misreadings, but Claude's paraphrase will sound plausible whether or not its internal interpretation matches yours on the ambiguous details; edge-case behavior like delimiter choice only becomes visible in concrete examples.
principle: concrete input/output examples beat prose for specifying transformations
relatedConcept: Iterative refinement starts by replacing ambiguous descriptions with 2-3 examples that make the expected behavior unmistakable.
overallExplanation: Concrete input/output examples beat prose for specifying transformations. Two or three representative pairs settle ambiguities that even carefully numbered prose leaves open.

objective: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
question: A backend developer must add a caching layer to a public-sector records API but has never built one: he cannot yet articulate requirements around invalidation, staleness tolerance, or failure behavior when the cache is down. He plans to prompt Claude Code with 'add Redis caching to the records service' and refine from there. What technique would surface the considerations he has not anticipated before implementation starts?
options: Use the interview pattern: have Claude ask him questions about invalidation strategy, failure modes, and consistency needs before writing any code
Write a test suite for the caching layer first, then let repeated test failures progressively teach both him and Claude what the requirements are
Provide a few input/output examples of cached versus uncached API responses so Claude can infer the intended caching behavior from the data
Prompt Claude to generate three alternative caching implementations and choose whichever one looks most complete after reviewing the code
optionExplanations: Correct. The interview pattern is designed for unfamiliar domains: Claude asks questions that surface considerations the developer has not anticipated — cache invalidation strategies, failure modes, staleness tolerance — so the design is informed before implementation begins.

Tempting because test-driven iteration is a powerful refinement technique, but it presumes you can already specify expected behavior and edge cases. He cannot write meaningful invalidation or failure-mode tests for requirements he has not yet discovered.

Tempting because examples excel at pinning down transformations, but caching correctness is about temporal behavior and failure policy, which response snapshots cannot express. This applies the right technique to the wrong kind of problem.

Tempting because comparing alternatives feels like exploration, but 'looks most complete' is exactly the judgment he lacks in an unfamiliar domain — he would be evaluating designs against requirements nobody has surfaced yet.
principle: in unfamiliar domains, let Claude interview you before implementing
relatedConcept: The interview pattern surfaces unanticipated design considerations, complementing test-driven iteration and worked examples.
overallExplanation: In unfamiliar domains, let Claude interview you before implementing. The interview pattern surfaces considerations like invalidation strategy and failure modes that the developer did not know to specify.

objective: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
question: A DevOps engineer is adding an automated review step to a GitHub Actions pipeline. The job must run Claude Code without any human present, and its findings must be machine-parseable so a script can post them as inline PR comments. On the first attempt the job hung waiting for input, and the output was free-form prose the script could not parse. Which two changes fix the integration? (Choose two.)
options: Run Claude Code with the -p (--print) flag so it executes the prompt non-interactively and exits instead of waiting for input
Use --output-format json together with --json-schema so findings are emitted as structured, machine-parseable output
Set the CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true environment variable in the workflow so the CLI detects it is running inside an automated pipeline
Instruct Claude in the prompt to respond only with valid JSON and have the posting script strip any surrounding prose before parsing
optionExplanations: Correct. The -p (or --print) flag is the documented mechanism for non-interactive mode: Claude Code processes the prompt, writes the result to stdout, and exits — which is exactly what prevents CI jobs from hanging on interactive input.

Correct. --output-format json with --json-schema enforces structured output at the CLI level, producing machine-parseable findings a script can reliably post as inline PR comments — no fragile prose parsing required.

Tempting because many CLIs use environment variables for CI detection, but CLAUDE_HEADLESS is not a Claude Code feature. Choosing it substitutes a plausible-sounding invention for the documented -p flag.

Tempting because prompt-level JSON instructions often help, but they are probabilistic — occasional prose or malformed output will still break the posting script. The CLI provides deterministic enforcement via --output-format json and --json-schema; use it instead of scraping.
principle: -p for non-interactive execution, --output-format json + --json-schema for parseable findings
relatedConcept: CI integration relies on Claude Code's headless CLI surface rather than prompt-level conventions.
overallExplanation: Use -p for non-interactive execution and --output-format json with --json-schema for machine-parseable findings. CI integrations should lean on the CLI's deterministic flags, not prompt-level output conventions.

objective: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
question: An e-commerce team's CI review bot re-runs Claude Code on every push to a pull request. Developers complain that after each new commit the bot re-posts the same findings it already raised, burying new feedback under duplicates; some reviews now carry four copies of one comment. How should the pipeline be changed to fix this?
options: Include the prior review's findings in the new run's context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
Deduplicate comments after the fact by string-matching each new finding against the text of comments already posted on the pull request
Run the review only once when the pull request is opened, so subsequent commits can never generate duplicate findings
Restrict each re-run to the lines changed in the newest commit so earlier findings fall outside the scope of the review
optionExplanations: Correct. Feeding prior findings into the re-run's context and instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues fixes duplication at the source: the model knows what has already been raised and can also confirm which earlier issues remain open.

Tempting because post-hoc deduplication seems simple, but Claude phrases the same finding differently across runs, so string matching both misses duplicates and can suppress genuinely new findings with similar wording. It patches the symptom downstream of the cause.

Tempting because it eliminates duplicates by construction, but it also eliminates review coverage for every commit after the first — precisely the pushes where regressions and fix-ups appear. The cure removes the pipeline's core value.

Tempting because scoping to the newest diff reduces repeat findings, but many defects — a broken cross-file contract, a regression in behavior introduced by the interaction of commits — are only visible with wider context. Narrowing scope trades duplicate noise for missed bugs.
principle: give re-runs the prior findings; ask only for new or unaddressed issues
relatedConcept: CI review quality depends on managing context across runs, not just on the single-run prompt.
overallExplanation: Give re-runs the prior findings and ask only for new or still-unaddressed issues. Duplicate comments are a context problem across runs, and the fix is supplying that context, not filtering output downstream.

objective: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
question: Claude Code follows your team's database-migration conventions perfectly in the tech lead's sessions, ignores them entirely for two other engineers on the same repository, and behaves inconsistently in the shared CI environment. Which two diagnostic steps most directly identify the cause? (Choose two.)
options: Run /memory in each environment to verify which memory files are actually being loaded into the session
Check whether the conventions live in the tech lead's user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md instead of project-level configuration shared through version control
Reinstall Claude Code on the two affected engineers' machines to rule out a corrupted local installation before investigating configuration
Ask the two engineers to restate the conventions in their prompts at the start of every session until the inconsistency resolves itself
optionExplanations: Correct. /memory is the diagnostic command for exactly this symptom: it shows which memory files are loaded in a given session, so comparing its output across the three environments immediately reveals whether the conventions file is present for the tech lead but absent for the others.

Correct. Instructions working for one user and failing for teammates is the signature of user-level configuration: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies only to that user and never travels through version control, so colleagues and CI receive nothing. Confirming the file's location pinpoints the hierarchy mistake and its fix.

Nothing in the symptom pattern suggests broken software — the tool works everywhere; only the loaded configuration differs. Reinstalling skips the configuration hierarchy, which explains per-user divergence exactly, and delays the two checks that actually diagnose it.

Manual restating is a workaround, not a diagnostic: it masks the symptom session by session while the misplaced configuration stays misplaced, and CI cannot restate anything. The goal is to find why loading differs, not to compensate by hand.
principle: diagnose loading with /memory, then check which hierarchy level holds the instructions
relatedConcept: Per-user behavioral divergence points to user-level vs project-level CLAUDE.md placement; /memory shows what each session loaded.
overallExplanation: Inconsistent instruction-following across users is diagnosed by verifying what loads (/memory) and where the instructions live (user-level files never propagate through version control). Reinstalls and manual prompt repetition address neither question.

objective: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
question: A payments team's single-package repository has a CLAUDE.md that has grown to 1,900 lines mixing testing standards, API conventions, and deployment procedures. Engineers struggle to review changes to it, and unrelated edits keep colliding in the one file. The content must all remain team-shared and loadable. What reorganization does the configuration system support for this?
options: Split the monolith into focused topic files in .claude/rules/ — such as testing.md, api-conventions.md, and deployment.md — as the modular alternative to one large CLAUDE.md
Move the full document unchanged into a single standards.md file and replace CLAUDE.md's content with one @import line referencing it
Compress the document by rewriting all 1,900 lines into terse bullet fragments so the single file becomes short enough to review comfortably
Distribute the three sections into each engineer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md according to which area of the codebase they most frequently work on
optionExplanations: Correct. The .claude/rules/ directory is the supported way to organize topic-specific rule files as an alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md. Each topic — testing, API conventions, deployment — becomes a focused, independently reviewable file, edits stop colliding, and everything stays project-scoped and shared through version control.

A single @import of the whole document is relocation, not modularization: the monolith survives intact in standards.md with the same review burden and the same edit collisions, just reachable through one extra hop. The problem was the file's structure, which this leaves untouched.

Compression trades clarity for length: conventions stripped to terse fragments lose the context that makes them followable, and the file still mixes three unrelated topics whose edits still collide. Line count was a symptom; the missing structure is the disease.

Scattering shared standards into personal user-level files destroys the property that matters most — team-wide consistency. User files never propagate through version control, engineers' copies drift immediately, and anyone touching an unfamiliar area works without that area's rules.
principle: organize topic-specific rules in .claude/rules/ instead of one monolith
relatedConcept: .claude/rules/ holds focused rule files (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md) as the modular alternative to a giant CLAUDE.md.
overallExplanation: Splitting a monolithic CLAUDE.md into focused topic files under .claude/rules/ is the supported modular organization: independently reviewable, collision-free, and still project-shared. Wholesale @import relocation, compression, and per-user scattering each miss the structural fix.

objective: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
question: In a product monorepo, the packages/mobile directory follows React Native conventions — navigation patterns, platform-split file rules, native module guidelines — that are meaningless in the web and backend packages. Universal engineering standards already live in the root CLAUDE.md. Where should the mobile conventions go so they apply when engineers work in that package?
options: In a CLAUDE.md file inside packages/mobile, using the directory level of the configuration hierarchy to scope the conventions to work in that subtree
In the root CLAUDE.md under a heading stating that the following section applies only when the files being edited belong to the mobile package
In each mobile engineer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, since they are the only developers who regularly work inside the mobile package's code
In a skill that mobile engineers invoke at the start of any session in which they expect to modify files inside the mobile package
optionExplanations: Correct. The CLAUDE.md hierarchy has a directory level for exactly this: a CLAUDE.md inside packages/mobile scopes the React Native conventions to work in that subtree, keeps them out of web and backend sessions, and remains version-controlled so every engineer who enters the package gets them automatically.

A conditional heading keeps the full mobile section loading into every session — web, backend, and all — and delegates the "applies only to mobile" decision to model inference on every task. Token cost stays universal and enforcement stays probabilistic when the hierarchy offers deterministic scoping.

User-level placement misdescribes the boundary: the conventions belong to a place in the repository, not to a set of people. Any non-mobile engineer touching the package gets no guidance, the copies drift across machines, and nothing reaches new team members on clone.

Skill invocation makes convention loading depend on memory — forget once and mobile code is generated without the platform rules. Always-applicable conventions for a code area deserve automatic loading tied to location, not an on-demand workflow trigger.
principle: directory-level CLAUDE.md scopes conventions to a subtree
relatedConcept: The hierarchy's directory level puts subtree-specific conventions where they load automatically for work in that location.
overallExplanation: Package-specific conventions belong in a directory-level CLAUDE.md inside that package: automatically loaded for work there, absent everywhere else, and shared via version control. Root-file headings, user files, and skills all scope by the wrong mechanism.

objective: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
question: A staff engineer wants Claude Code to always follow her personal working style — concise explanations, commit messages in her preferred format, and her habit of running tests before any commit — across the dozen repositories she contributes to, without imposing any of it on teammates or appearing in any repository. Where does this configuration belong?
options: In her user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies to all of her sessions across every project while remaining invisible to teammates
In each of the twelve repositories' project CLAUDE.md files, marked with a comment noting the preferences are hers and optional for others
In a .claude/rules/ file with a paths glob broad enough to match every file, added to whichever repository she is currently working in
In a personal skill she invokes at the start of each session to load her preferences into the conversation before beginning any work
optionExplanations: Correct. User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is precisely the scope described: it applies to that user's sessions in every project on her machine and is never shared through version control, so personal style preferences follow her everywhere without touching teammates or repositories.

Project CLAUDE.md files load for everyone who clones the repository — an "optional, personal" comment does not stop Claude from applying the instructions in every teammate's session. It also means maintaining the same preferences in twelve places and pushing personal style into shared review.

A match-everything rule file committed to a repository is project-scoped by definition: teammates receive her personal preferences, reviewers must approve them, and she must replicate the file across all twelve repositories. Every property of the requirement points away from repository placement.

A skill loads only when invoked, so any session where she forgets the incantation runs without her preferences — the opposite of "always." Always-on personal configuration is what the user level of the hierarchy exists for; on-demand invocation is the wrong loading model.
principle: personal, cross-project, always-on preferences belong at the user level
relatedConcept: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies to one user across all projects and never propagates to teammates via version control.
overallExplanation: Personal preferences that should follow one engineer across every project — and never reach teammates — are exactly what user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md scopes. Project files and rules are shared by design, and skills load only on invocation.

objective: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
question: Your database team codified a multi-step migration procedure — schema diff, backfill plan, rollback script, reviewer checklist — and wants it available as a /generate-migration slash command to every engineer automatically when they clone or pull the repository. Where must the command file be created for that distribution model?
options: In the .claude/commands/ directory of the repository, so the command ships with the project through version control
In ~/.claude/commands/ on each engineer's machine, with the onboarding guide instructing new hires to copy the file there manually
In the project CLAUDE.md as a documented procedure section, since always-loaded memory makes a separate command file unnecessary
In .claude/skills/ on the tech lead's machine, shared with the team by exporting the skill whenever the procedure changes
optionExplanations: Correct. Project-scoped commands live in .claude/commands/ inside the repository, which is exactly what makes them team-wide: version control distributes the command to every engineer on clone or pull, updates propagate like any other change, and the procedure gets reviewed alongside code.

User-scoped ~/.claude/commands/ is for personal commands — distributing a team asset this way makes onboarding manual, guarantees stale copies as the procedure evolves, and gives version control no role in propagating updates. The scope contradicts the distribution requirement.

CLAUDE.md is always-loaded context, so a once-a-week multi-step procedure would tax every session's tokens while providing no invocation mechanism — engineers still could not run /generate-migration. On-demand workflows belong in commands, not in universal memory.

A skill living on one person's machine is not shared tooling: export-on-change is a manual distribution chore that version control already solves, and any lapse leaves the team running divergent versions of a procedure whose consistency is the whole point.
principle: team-shared slash commands live in the repo's .claude/commands/
relatedConcept: Project-scoped commands distribute through version control; ~/.claude/commands/ is for personal, unshared commands.
overallExplanation: Commands the whole team should receive on clone belong in the repository's .claude/commands/ directory, where version control handles distribution and review. Home-directory copies, CLAUDE.md prose, and manual skill exports all break the automatic-distribution requirement.

objective: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
question: Your team's /scaffold-service skill generates a new microservice from two required inputs: the service name and its type (worker, api, or stream). Engineers keep invoking it bare — just /scaffold-service — and the skill proceeds with guessed defaults, producing wrongly named services that must be deleted and regenerated. Which frontmatter change addresses this?
options: Add argument-hint to the SKILL.md frontmatter so engineers are prompted for the required parameters when they invoke the skill without arguments
Add context: fork to the SKILL.md frontmatter so the scaffolding runs in an isolated sub-agent context where wrong guesses cannot pollute the session
Add allowed-tools to the SKILL.md frontmatter restricting the skill to read-only tools so it cannot create files until the arguments are supplied
Rename the skill to /scaffold-service-name-type so the required parameters are visible in the command name engineers type at invocation
optionExplanations: Correct. argument-hint is the frontmatter option for exactly this failure: when developers invoke the skill without arguments, it prompts them for the required parameters — service name and type — instead of letting the skill proceed on guessed defaults. The wasted generate-delete-regenerate cycle disappears at the invocation step.

context: fork addresses output isolation — keeping verbose or exploratory skill output from polluting the main conversation. The problem here is missing inputs at invocation, which forking does nothing about: the isolated skill would still scaffold a wrongly named service from guesses.

allowed-tools restricts which tools a skill may use during execution; it is a safety boundary, not an input-collection mechanism. A read-only restriction would break the skill's legitimate purpose — creating files — rather than prompting anyone for the missing name and type.

Encoding parameter names into the command name documents the requirement but enforces nothing: a bare invocation still runs, still guesses, and still produces a service that must be deleted. The frontmatter offers a real prompting mechanism; a longer name is a hint without teeth.
principle: argument-hint prompts for required parameters at invocation
relatedConcept: SKILL.md frontmatter roles: argument-hint collects inputs, context: fork isolates output, allowed-tools bounds execution.
overallExplanation: Skills invoked without their required inputs need argument-hint frontmatter, which prompts the developer for parameters instead of proceeding on guesses. Forking isolates output and allowed-tools bounds execution — neither collects the missing arguments.

objective: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
question: An engineer relies on the team's shared release-notes skill from .claude/skills/ but wants a stricter personal version: extra security-change callouts and a different section order. Her teammates want the shared skill exactly as it is. How should she set up her customized version without disrupting anyone?
options: Create a personal variant in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name, leaving the shared project skill untouched for the rest of the team
Edit the shared skill in .claude/skills/ directly, since her stricter format is a superset and teammates will benefit from the added callouts
Create a skill with the identical name in ~/.claude/skills/ so her user-scoped copy quietly takes precedence over the project version in her sessions
Maintain a long-lived local branch of the repository where the shared skill file carries her modifications, rebasing it as the team's version evolves
optionExplanations: Correct. Personal skill customization is done by creating a variant in ~/.claude/skills/ with a different name, precisely to avoid affecting teammates. She invokes her stricter version by its own name, the shared skill stays untouched for the team, and no repository change or coordination is needed.

"Superset" is her judgment, not the team's decision: editing the shared skill pushes her section order and extra callouts into every teammate's release notes without agreement, and version control turns a personal preference into a reviewed team change nobody requested.

Deliberately shadowing the shared name invites confusion the different-name guidance exists to prevent: her sessions silently run different behavior under the same invocation teammates use, team updates to the shared skill stop reaching her, and debugging "why do our outputs differ" becomes a hunt.

A permanently diverged branch is heavy machinery for a personal preference: every rebase risks conflicts in a file she does not own, accidental pushes leak her variant to the team, and the user-scoped skills directory already exists to hold exactly this kind of personal tooling.
principle: personal skill variants go in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name
relatedConcept: Personal customization of shared skills uses user-scoped variants with distinct names so teammates are unaffected.
overallExplanation: Customize shared skills by creating a personal variant in ~/.claude/skills/ with a different name — teammates keep the untouched project skill, and no shadowing or branch divergence enters the picture. Same-name overrides and direct edits both create silent behavioral drift.

objective: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
question: Your team's /explore-alternatives skill brainstorms architecture options for a named component, generating long chains of exploratory reasoning. Two complaints have surfaced: the speculative output floods the main conversation and lingers in context long after a direction is chosen, and engineers who invoke it bare get brainstorming about a component the skill guessed. Which two frontmatter options fix these issues? (Choose two.)
options: context: fork, so the exploratory brainstorming runs in an isolated sub-agent context instead of polluting the main conversation
argument-hint, so engineers invoking the skill without naming a component are prompted for the required parameter
allowed-tools, restricting the skill to file-write operations so its speculative reasoning cannot trigger destructive actions
Moving the skill to ~/.claude/skills/, so each engineer's brainstorming stays isolated inside their own personal configuration
optionExplanations: Correct. context: fork is the frontmatter option for skills that produce exploratory context — like brainstorming alternatives — running them in an isolated sub-agent context so speculative reasoning never enters the main session. Only the useful conclusion comes back, and chosen-direction sessions stay clean.

Correct. argument-hint handles the bare-invocation failure: when the skill is invoked without arguments, the engineer is prompted for the required component name instead of the skill guessing. The two frontmatter options address the two complaints exactly.

allowed-tools is a real frontmatter option but aims at a problem nobody reported: no destructive actions occurred, and restricting to file-write operations does nothing about context flooding or missing arguments. It is the right mechanism for a different failure mode.

Relocating the skill to user scope changes who has it, not how it behaves: each engineer's main conversation still floods with speculative output, bare invocations still guess, and the team loses the shared, version-controlled skill in the bargain.
principle: fork isolates exploratory output; argument-hint collects required inputs
relatedConcept: context: fork suits brainstorming skills whose speculative context should not persist in the main session; argument-hint fixes bare invocations.
overallExplanation: Brainstorming skills pair context: fork — isolating exploratory reasoning in a sub-agent so the main conversation stays clean — with argument-hint, which prompts for the required component when invoked bare. allowed-tools and user-scoping solve different problems.

objective: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
question: Your REST conventions — response envelope shape, pagination contract, error code registry — govern handler code in two places: src/api/ and services/gateway/src/routes/. They currently sit in the root CLAUDE.md, loading into every session including frontend work. How do you scope them to load only when editing handler code in either location?
options: Create one .claude/rules/ file with YAML frontmatter listing both globs, paths: ["src/api/**/*", "services/gateway/src/routes/**/*"], so it activates for matching files in either tree
Place duplicate CLAUDE.md files inside src/api/ and services/gateway/src/routes/, each containing a full copy of the REST conventions text
Keep the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md but move them under a heading instructing Claude to apply the section only during API-related tasks
Create a rules file with the single glob paths: ["**/api/**"], relying on both directories containing the substring "api" somewhere in their paths
optionExplanations: Correct. A .claude/rules/ file's YAML frontmatter paths field takes multiple glob patterns, so one rule file can activate for both directory trees. The conventions live in a single maintained place, load only when matching files are edited, and stay out of frontend sessions entirely.

Duplicate directory-level files do scope correctly, but at the price path rules exist to avoid: two full copies of the conventions to keep synchronized, with drift guaranteed the first time someone updates one and forgets the other. One rule file with two globs has no such failure mode.

An instruction-scoped heading still loads the full conventions into every session — frontend included — spending the tokens the change was meant to save, and it makes application depend on the model's per-task inference rather than deterministic path matching.

The gateway routes directory does contain "api" in neither of its segments — services/gateway/src/routes/ would never match — and substring-driven globs also overmatch unrelated paths like src/api-docs/. Globs should state the intended trees explicitly, not gamble on naming coincidences.
principle: one rule file can scope to multiple trees via a list of paths globs
relatedConcept: The YAML frontmatter paths field accepts multiple glob patterns, avoiding duplicated directory-level convention copies.
overallExplanation: A single .claude/rules/ file with both globs in its paths frontmatter scopes the conventions to exactly the two handler trees — one maintained copy, deterministic loading, zero cost to unrelated sessions. Duplicated files drift and prose headings still load everywhere.

objective: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
question: An engineer created .claude/rules/terraform.md with frontmatter paths: ["terraform/*"] to load infrastructure conventions conditionally. The rule works when editing terraform/main.tf but never activates for terraform/modules/vpc/main.tf or anything else under the module subdirectories, where most of the team's work happens. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
options: The single-level glob terraform/* matches only files directly under terraform/; change it to terraform/**/* so files in nested subdirectories also match
Rules files activate only for the directory containing .claude/; move the rules directory into terraform/ so the conventions attach to that subtree
The paths field requires each directory to be listed individually; enumerate every module subdirectory in the list and update it as modules are added
Conditional rules cannot match nested paths at all; move the Terraform conventions back into the root CLAUDE.md where they load unconditionally
optionExplanations: Correct. This is glob semantics: terraform/* matches a single path segment, so only files immediately under terraform/ activate the rule, while nested files like terraform/modules/vpc/main.tf need the recursive pattern. Changing the frontmatter to terraform/**/* makes the rule fire for the whole subtree, which is what the team intended.

The rules mechanism is not location-bound in that way — .claude/rules/ files scope by their paths globs, not by where the directory sits. Relocating configuration into the Terraform tree adds a nonstandard layout while leaving the actual defect, the non-recursive glob, unfixed.

Enumerating every module directory works today and breaks with the next module added — a silent gap each time the tree grows. Glob patterns exist precisely so one recursive expression covers current and future subdirectories without a maintenance treadmill.

Nested matching works fine with the right pattern, so retreating to unconditional loading surrenders the entire benefit: Terraform conventions back in every frontend and backend session, tokens spent everywhere, for a defect one glob character pair fixes.
principle: use recursive globs (dir/**/*) when conventions cover a whole subtree
relatedConcept: Single-segment globs match one level; **/ patterns are what make path-scoped rules cover nested directories.
overallExplanation: terraform/* is a single-level glob, so nested module files never match; the recursive terraform/**/* covers the whole subtree. Relocating the rules directory, enumerating subdirectories, or abandoning conditional loading all misdiagnose a one-pattern fix.

objective: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
question: A platform team is decomposing its root CLAUDE.md. Two convention sets need conditional loading: SQL migration rules for files under db/migrations/, and MDX documentation style rules for .mdx files scattered through every feature directory in the repository. Which two statements correctly describe how to implement this with path-specific rules? (Choose two.)
options: Create .claude/rules/ files with YAML frontmatter paths globs so each convention set loads only when Claude edits files matching its patterns
Use a file-type glob such as **/*.mdx for the documentation rules, since glob patterns apply conventions by type regardless of directory location
Register each rules file in the root CLAUDE.md with an @import line, since rules files only activate after being imported into the main memory file
Place a CLAUDE.md in every feature directory that contains .mdx files, since per-directory files are how scattered file types receive conventions
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the path-specific rules mechanism: files in .claude/rules/ carry YAML frontmatter paths fields with glob patterns, and each rule loads only when editing files matching its globs — SQL rules for db/migrations/**, MDX rules for their own pattern — cutting irrelevant context from every other session.

Correct. Glob patterns are the right scoping for conventions that follow a file type across the tree: **/*.mdx activates the documentation rules wherever an MDX file lives, exactly the advantage path-specific rules hold over directory-bound configuration for scattered files.

No import registration step exists for rule activation — .claude/rules/ files with paths frontmatter activate on their own when matching files are edited. @import is a separate modularity mechanism for composing CLAUDE.md content, not a prerequisite for rules.

Per-directory CLAUDE.md files would mean duplicating the MDX style rules across every feature directory and adding another copy each time docs appear somewhere new — the exact maintenance burden the glob-pattern approach exists to eliminate for scattered file types.
principle: rules scope by frontmatter globs; file-type patterns follow scattered files
relatedConcept: .claude/rules/ + paths globs load conventions conditionally; **/*.ext patterns beat per-directory files for spread-out types.
overallExplanation: Path-specific rules are self-activating: .claude/rules/ files with paths frontmatter load when matching files are edited, and file-type globs like **/*.mdx follow scattered files anywhere in the tree. No @import registration exists, and per-directory duplication is the anti-pattern globs replace.

objective: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
question: Enthusiastic after adopting path-specific rules, a team moves everything out of CLAUDE.md — including universal security requirements and core coding standards that genuinely apply to every file — into .claude/rules/ files, giving those universal ones paths: ["**/*"]. A reviewer questions the design. What is the right division?
options: Keep universal, always-applicable standards in the project CLAUDE.md and use path-scoped rules for conventions tied to specific file types or code areas
Keep everything as rules files, since a paths: ["**/*"] rule loads more efficiently than the equivalent content placed in the project CLAUDE.md
Move the universal standards into each developer's user-level configuration so the project's rules directory contains only path-scoped conventions
Convert the universal standards into a skill invoked at session start, keeping both CLAUDE.md and the rules directory reserved for scoped content
optionExplanations: Correct. The mechanisms divide by applicability: CLAUDE.md is the home for universal, always-loaded standards, while path-scoped rules earn their value by activating conditionally for specific file types or areas. A match-everything rule gains nothing from the rules mechanism — conditional loading that never excludes anything is just indirection.

There is no efficiency gain: a rule matching every file loads for every edit exactly as CLAUDE.md content does, with the same token cost. The claim mistakes the mechanism for the benefit — savings come from conventions not loading where irrelevant, which **/* forfeits by construction.

User-level placement breaks the team property that universal standards most need: nothing propagates through version control, so each developer's copy drifts and new engineers clone a repository whose security requirements exist only on veterans' machines.

A session-start skill makes universal standards contingent on someone remembering to invoke them — forget once and code is generated without the security requirements. Always-applicable content needs the always-loaded mechanism, which is precisely what CLAUDE.md provides.
principle: universal standards stay in CLAUDE.md; rules are for genuinely scoped conventions
relatedConcept: Path-scoped rules pay off through conditional loading; a **/* rule is CLAUDE.md content wearing a costume.
overallExplanation: The division is by applicability: universal standards belong in always-loaded CLAUDE.md, and path-specific rules are for conventions scoped to file types or areas. A paths: ["**/*"] rule loads everywhere anyway, so it adds indirection without any conditional-loading benefit.

objective: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
question: A production incident traces to one function: a stack trace shows the payment validator throwing on records whose expiry date field is null, and the fix is an added conditional in that single file. The on-call engineer's team habitually opens plan mode for every Claude Code task, and she asks whether this one needs it. What do you advise?
options: Use direct execution — this is a well-scoped single-file fix with a clear stack trace, exactly the profile where plan mode adds overhead without value
Use plan mode anyway, since payment code is business-critical and critical code paths always justify the extra exploration phase before any change
Use plan mode with the Explore subagent first to map every caller of the validator before deciding whether the conditional is the right fix
Split the work between modes: plan the conditional's placement in plan mode, then switch to direct execution to type the actual change into the file
optionExplanations: Correct. Direct execution is appropriate for simple, well-scoped changes — a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace, adding a validation conditional, is the canonical example. Plan mode's value lies in large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, and architectural decisions, none of which this fix presents.

Criticality does not change the decision criteria: plan mode is selected for scope and approach ambiguity, not for the importance of the code. A one-conditional fix has one obvious approach; the safeguard critical code deserves here is a test for the null case, not a planning phase with nothing to plan.

The Explore subagent exists to isolate verbose discovery during genuinely large investigations. Mapping every caller to add a null guard indicated by a specific stack trace is ceremony — the failing path is already identified, and the fix does not change the function's contract for other callers.

Mode-splitting is the right pattern for large migrations where investigation precedes a multi-file implementation. Applied to a one-line conditional it is pure overhead: the "plan" is a sentence, and the transition costs more than the decision it formalizes.
principle: well-scoped single-file fixes with clear diagnostics take direct execution
relatedConcept: Plan mode earns its cost on scale and approach ambiguity; a stack-trace-guided one-file fix has neither.
overallExplanation: A single-file fix with a clear stack trace is direct execution's canonical case — plan mode's criteria are large-scale change, multiple valid approaches, and architectural implications, none present here. Criticality argues for a regression test, not a planning phase.

objective: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
question: Your team must sync inventory data to a new fulfillment partner. Two viable designs exist — an event-driven push through the message queue, or a scheduled batch pull — with different infrastructure requirements for queue capacity, retry handling, and monitoring. An engineer wants to start coding the event-driven version immediately since it was mentioned first. What do you recommend?
options: Enter plan mode to explore the existing codebase and compare both integration approaches before committing to either implementation
Proceed with direct execution on the event-driven design, since working code will reveal any infrastructure problems faster than analysis can
Implement thin prototypes of both designs in direct execution and keep whichever one reaches a working end-to-end sync first
Ask Claude in a single prompt to declare which approach is better and then implement the winner immediately in the same session
optionExplanations: Correct. Choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure requirements is a signature plan mode case: safe exploration of the codebase and a deliberate comparison happen before any code is committed, preventing the costly rework of discovering mid-build that the wrong architecture was chosen.

"First mentioned" is not a selection criterion, and infrastructure mismatches — queue capacity, retry semantics — surface after substantial build investment, when switching means discarding working code. Direct execution fits well-understood changes, not unmade architectural decisions.

Racing two prototypes doubles the build cost to answer a question exploration answers cheaply, and "first to work end-to-end" measures implementation ease rather than operational fit — retry behavior and monitoring burden appear in production, not in a thin prototype.

A one-prompt verdict skips the ingredient that makes the comparison meaningful: exploration of this codebase's actual queue usage, load patterns, and operational tooling. Plan mode exists to ground the recommendation in the code before implementation locks it in.
principle: competing approaches with infrastructure implications call for plan mode first
relatedConcept: Plan mode's criteria include choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure requirements.
overallExplanation: When two viable designs carry different infrastructure requirements, plan mode's explore-and-compare phase is the cheap way to choose before code hardens the decision. Building first, racing prototypes, or a context-free verdict all defer the comparison until it is expensive.

objective: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
question: An engineer ran a thorough plan mode session for an ORM migration: Claude explored the codebase, compared approaches, and produced a detailed migration plan she fully approves. She keeps prompting in plan mode expecting the repository files to start changing, but nothing is ever modified. What should she understand about the workflow?
options: Plan mode is for exploration and design without committing changes; the intended workflow is to approve the plan and proceed to direct execution for implementation
Plan mode applies its accumulated changes in a single batch only after the session ends, so she should close the session and let the edits flush to disk
The plan must first be saved into CLAUDE.md so implementation sessions can load it as context before any file modification is permitted to begin
File modification stays locked until the plan is exported as a custom slash command, which is the artifact Claude Code executes against the repository
optionExplanations: Correct. Plan mode's purpose is safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes — by design it does not modify files. The documented workflow combines the two modes: plan the approach in plan mode, then execute the approved plan with direct implementation. Her plan is done; the next step is switching modes.

No end-of-session batch application exists — plan mode never queues edits for later. Closing the session would simply discard her momentum; the plan is a design artifact to carry into direct execution, not a transaction waiting to commit.

No such persistence gate exists: nothing requires a plan to pass through CLAUDE.md before implementation. CLAUDE.md holds standing project instructions; the approved plan flows into implementation directly by continuing into direct execution.

Slash commands are reusable prompt workflows, not compiled plan artifacts, and no export step gates file modification. The mechanism this option invents replaces a simple mode switch with machinery Claude Code does not have.
principle: plan mode designs without modifying; implementation happens in direct execution
relatedConcept: The combined workflow: plan mode for investigation and approach choice, then direct execution to implement the approved plan.
overallExplanation: Plan mode intentionally makes no file changes — it is the safe exploration and design phase. The intended workflow pairs it with direct execution: approve the plan, switch modes, implement. No batch flush, CLAUDE.md gate, or command export is involved.

objective: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
question: Your team is triaging four upcoming Claude Code tasks and deciding which ones warrant plan mode before implementation begins, based on scope, architectural weight, and how many valid approaches each task admits. Which two of these tasks should start in plan mode? (Choose two.)
options: Restructuring the monolith's order-processing module into two services, with open questions about where the transactional boundary should sit
Replacing the deprecated logging library across roughly 60 files, where two viable integration approaches differ in their infrastructure demands
Fixing a null-pointer exception in one utility function, pinpointed by a stack trace from last night's error monitoring alert
Adding a date-range validation conditional to a single reporting endpoint that currently accepts end dates earlier than start dates
optionExplanations: Correct. Service decomposition is architectural work with an unresolved design question — where the transactional boundary sits — and broad blast radius. That combination of architectural implications and multiple valid answers is precisely what plan mode's exploration phase is for.

Correct. A 60-file library migration with two viable integration approaches carrying different infrastructure demands matches plan mode's criteria on both axes: large-scale multi-file change and an approach decision that must be made before implementation to avoid rework across every touched file.

A stack-trace-pinpointed null-pointer fix in one function is direct execution's textbook case: the scope is one file, the diagnosis is done, and there is essentially one way to write the guard. A planning phase would have nothing to decide.

A single-endpoint validation conditional is the guide's own example of a simple, well-scoped change suited to direct execution — clear requirement, one obvious implementation, no architectural surface. Plan mode would add ceremony without reducing any risk.
principle: plan mode for architectural scope and approach ambiguity; direct execution for pinpointed fixes
relatedConcept: Selection criteria: multi-file scale, multiple valid approaches, architectural implications — versus well-scoped single-file changes.
overallExplanation: The service split and the 60-file migration carry architectural weight and competing approaches — plan mode territory. The stack-traced null fix and the single-endpoint validation are well-scoped direct-execution changes where planning has nothing to decide.

objective: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
question: A data team is iterating with Claude Code on a CSV normalization module. Feedback each round is impressionistic — "still chokes on weird rows," "the quoting is off again" — and fixes for new cases keep silently breaking previously working ones, with nobody able to say exactly which behaviors have regressed. What refinement approach fixes this loop?
options: Write a test suite covering expected behavior, edge cases, and performance requirements first, then iterate by sharing the specific test failures with Claude
Continue the conversational refinement but require reviewers to describe each defect in at least a paragraph so Claude receives richer prose context
Restart from scratch in a fresh session each round so accumulated confusion from earlier iterations cannot influence the next version of the module
Switch to plan mode so Claude designs the complete normalization architecture upfront before any further code is written or revised
optionExplanations: Correct. Test-driven iteration is the named technique for this failure: the suite pins down expected behavior, edge cases, and performance requirements as executable facts, every iteration is guided by concrete failing tests instead of impressions, and regressions surface instantly because previously passing tests break visibly.

Longer prose is still prose: "the quoting is off again" in paragraph form remains unverifiable and unanchored, and nothing detects when a fix for one complaint reverses an earlier one. The loop's defect is the absence of executable criteria, not insufficient word count.

Fresh sessions discard the problem's history without recording it — the new session re-learns requirements from the same impressionistic feedback and re-breaks the same undocumented behaviors. Regression protection requires persisted expectations, which tests provide and session resets do not.

Plan mode addresses approach selection before large or ambiguous work; this module's design is settled and the failures are behavioral edge cases discovered over time. An upfront architecture pass produces no mechanism for catching the next regression, which is the actual complaint.
principle: write the test suite first; iterate by sharing failures
relatedConcept: Test-driven iteration converts vague feedback into failing tests that guide fixes and expose regressions immediately.
overallExplanation: Test-driven iteration fixes both reported problems at once: a suite covering expected behavior and edge cases turns vague complaints into specific failures to share, and previously working behavior is guarded because regressions break visible tests. Prose volume and fresh sessions guard nothing.

objective: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
question: A review of Claude-generated connection-pool code found three defects: the retry logic can double-acquire connections, the timeout handling leaks them under load, and the pool-exhaustion path deadlocks with the retry behavior. The team fixed them one per iteration, and each fix has broken one of the other two areas twice now. How should the next iteration be run?
options: Present all three issues together in one detailed message, since the fixes interact and must be reasoned about jointly rather than sequentially
Continue one fix per iteration but reverse the order, addressing the deadlock first since it is the most severe of the three defects
Open three parallel sessions, one per defect, and merge the three resulting patches once each session has produced its isolated fix
Ask Claude to rewrite the entire connection pool from scratch, since three defects in one component indicate the generation is unsalvageable
optionExplanations: Correct. The rule is to match batching to issue coupling: interacting problems belong in a single detailed message so the model reasons about all constraints jointly, while sequential fixing suits independent issues. Retry, timeout, and exhaustion behavior share connection-lifecycle state — the observed fix-one-break-another cycle is the signature of coupled fixes applied separately.

Reordering does not decouple: whichever defect is fixed first, its fix still alters lifecycle behavior the other two depend on, and the regression cycle continues. Severity determines urgency, not the batching strategy that coupling dictates.

Parallel sessions maximize the interaction problem — three fixes to the same shared-state component designed with zero mutual awareness, merged blind. The merge point is exactly where double-acquires and deadlocks would be reintroduced.

Three related defects in intricate concurrency code do not make the component unsalvageable, and a rewrite discards behavior already validated while re-rolling the dice on fresh defects. The failure was iteration strategy, not the generation itself.
principle: interacting issues go in one message; sequential fixing is for independent ones
relatedConcept: Batching strategy follows issue coupling: joint reasoning for interacting fixes, sequential iteration for unrelated ones.
overallExplanation: When fixes interact — here through shared connection-lifecycle state — present all issues in a single detailed message so they are reasoned about jointly. Sequential fixing suits independent problems; applied to coupled ones it produces exactly this fix-one-break-another cycle.

objective: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
question: Your legacy-data migration script mishandles records with null fields: Claude's version fabricates a default date of birth and an empty-string middle name instead of propagating the nulls to the new schema. Two rounds of prose correction — "never invent values for missing fields" — have not fully fixed the behavior. What should the next iteration include?
options: Specific test cases with example input records containing null fields and the exact expected output showing nulls preserved in the new schema
A sterner restatement of the rule, elevated to the top of the prompt in bold, stating that fabricating values is strictly forbidden in all cases
The interview pattern, having Claude ask clarifying questions about the migration's requirements before attempting another revision of the script
A fresh session with only the original migration specification, removing the accumulated correction attempts that may be confusing the model
optionExplanations: Correct.
